Le 23 septembre prochain, à l’ouverture: On September 23, at the opening of the new parliamentary session, the Governor General will deliver the Speech from the Throne. In it, the government is expected to mention incorporating the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) into Canadian law. UNDRIP remains a hot potato, however, between Indigenous peoples and the Canadian government.
Marlene Hale, membre de la nation wet’su: Marlene Hale, a member of the Wet’suwet’en Nation who has lived in Quebec for several years, is not very enthusiastic about the Speech from the Throne. “[The prime minister] needs to come out of hiding and do the right thing. He wore our clothes, he ate our food, he sat down with our chiefs and he lied to us,” she says, referring to Justin Trudeau’s decision to give the green light to the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion.
« La DNUDPA, c’est d’abord la reconnaiss: “UNDRIP is first of all the recognition that we are human beings – and that we are peoples. We have the rights of peoples – fundamental rights to land and natural resources,” says Kenneth Deer, a member of the Kahnawake community who has worked on the declaration since the very beginning and served as co-chair of the Indigenous Caucus at the United Nations. In his view, implementing it could improve the lives of Indigenous peoples in Canada by granting them sovereign rights – which would contradict the current Indian Act. “In the Mohawk territory of Kahnawake, it would mean an economy based on the resources of the land, and sharing those resources to develop that economy and the services needed for the Mohawk nation to function well.”
« Nous ne demandons pas de gouverner tou: “We are not asking to govern everyone on our territory – it stretches from Tiohtiake to New York State and the north shore of Lake Ontario – but to exercise our autonomy and apply our laws so that we can live well together, nation to nation,” he adds. “We recognize Canada’s right to self-determination. We want the same rights.”
Au sujet de la mise en œuvre de la DNUDP: On the implementation of UNDRIP, Mr. Deer believes it could bring real change. But he fears that its application will change its deeper meaning. The continued oppression of Indigenous peoples through existing Canadian laws and policies gives him no reason to believe that UNDRIP will be implemented in good faith. As for Emilio Wawatie, a young hunter and member of the Rapid Lake community, he believes UNDRIP can have positive effects for him and his community, as well as for relations between occupants and Indigenous people.
« Nous voulons être entendus. Nous voulo: “We want to be heard. We want to be respected,” says the Anishinaabe hunter simply, whose territorial rights and resources are the subject of dispute.
Enfin, d’après Eriel Deranger, directric: Finally, according to Eriel Deranger, founder and executive director of Indigenous Climate Action, the Declaration has the potential to act as a guide for governments, particularly on all questions relating to resources and land, in the interest of future generations. Canada currently has third-party interests with corporations, notably in the Trans Mountain pipeline, the Site C dam and various liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects. The climate justice activist believes this puts the government in a conflict of interest with respect to Indigenous land rights.
« Il y a des corporations avec lesquelle: “There are corporations with which Canada has long-standing interests. The country has agreements and business relationships that it considers indissoluble. And we have a long-standing relationship with our land,” Ms. Deranger points out. “It’s no longer simply an issue of control over territory, it’s a question of survival for our communities, our cultures, our languages and our traditions – because these are deeply tied to the places we come from.”
Le rapport entre les droits autochtones: The relationship between Indigenous rights and hydrocarbon development in Canada essentially involves laws affecting land. Territorial disputes – from the Wet’suwet’en case to the Site C dam project, by way of the Muskrat Falls generating station in Labrador and LNG projects – highlight governments’ determination to pursue major projects on Indigenous territories and to impose development policies that run counter to the well-being and interests of Indigenous communities. British Columbia adopted UNDRIP in November 2019.
En février dernier, les chefs héréditair: Last February, the hereditary chiefs of the Wet’suwet’en Nation in British Columbia asserted their authority by blocking access for Coastal GasLink pipeline workers on their unceded territory. In response, an injunction from the Supreme Court of British Columbia led to the deployment of the RCMP and its armed intervention against Indigenous resistance camps, an intervention that sparked a wave of solidarity blockades across the country and slowed several sectors of the Canadian economy.
Le 14 mai dernier, le Canada, la Colombi: On May 14, Canada, British Columbia and the Wet’suwet’en hereditary chiefs signed a <l1>memorandum of understanding</l1> recognizing the Wet’suwet’en Nation’s Indigenous rights and title. British Columbia also passed <l2>Bill 41</l2> on UNDRIP, Article 32 of which states that the state must “obtain free, prior and informed consent” from Indigenous peoples before approving any development project on their territory. On this point, however, Kenneth Deer remains cautious.
« Le Canada peut intervenir sur ces terr: “Canada can intervene on these territories if it decides it’s in Canada’s interest. The memorandum of understanding is not an absolute protection of the land,” he says. Russ Diabo, a member of the Mohawk Nation and a First Nations policy analyst, agrees. “UNDRIP is a declaration, not a convention.
Elle n’a pas force de loi, mais sert plu: It doesn’t have the force of law, but serves instead as inspiration for the government – which is not very reassuring.” To him, this can only mean one thing: “Canada is trying to domesticate Indigenous peoples and international law, so it can act in violation of international rights.”
Une <l1>recherche mandatée</l1> par l’As: <l1>Research commissioned</l1> by the Assembly of First Nations found that a majority of Canadians support the Government of Canada taking legislative measures to implement UNDRIP.
Selon l’attaché de presse du ministre de: According to the Minister of Justice’s press secretary, the Government of Canada has made a commitment to advance the rights of Inuit, Métis and First Nations.
« Alors que nous marchons ensemble sur l: “As we walk together on the path of reconciliation, we have committed to introducing legislation to implement UNDRIP before the end of 2020, working closely with national Indigenous organizations,” the government replied to our interview request.
Malgré l’apparente bonne foi d’Ottawa, l: Despite Ottawa’s apparent good faith, Indigenous experts and leaders are not convinced. Roméo Saganash, a Cree lawyer and politician, worked for nearly four decades on the development of UNDRIP. In 2018, while he was MP for the <l1>riding of Abitibi—Baie-James—Nunavik—Eeyou</l1>, he tabled Bill C-262, on implementing the Declaration in Canada. The bill died on the Order Paper in the Senate. “I sat in the House of Commons for eight years, and the rights guaranteed by the Declaration are constantly being challenged by our own parliamentarians. We have to insist that Indigenous rights are human rights,” he explains.
Aujourd’hui, l’ancien député fédéral aim: Today, the former federal MP would like to be able to offer his comments to the parliamentary committee responsible for implementing UNDRIP.
Saganash juge que les droits autochtones: Saganash believes the Government of Canada does not recognize the Indigenous rights set out in the Declaration as human rights. “The price of freedom and Indigenous rights is our vigilance,” he continues. “Canada does not respect the rule of law. The rule of law doesn’t mean sending in the police to remove a barricade. The rule of law is respecting and upholding constitutional law.”
Cette position est en partie partagée pa: This position is partly shared by Kenneth Deer, who says he is worried “in the face of institutionalized racism” in a country about to implement UNDRIP. “It sometimes comes out in language and attitudes. There is an enormous bureaucracy used to oppressing Indigenous peoples, and that oppression is based on feelings of racial superiority.”
<sup>Au Québec, la communication ne pass: <sup>In Quebec, communication simply isn’t getting through, even though the Quebec government and the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador say they are reaching out to each other.</sup> It is therefore hard to predict how things will unfold. It should be recalled that the National Assembly passed a motion in favour of implementing UNDRIP in October 2019, but that Premier François Legault has said he does not want to give Indigenous peoples a veto over any question of economic development.
« Le gouvernement du Québec adhère aux p: “The Government of Quebec adheres to the principles of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). To give meaning to this Declaration, we must have a shared understanding of its content, and we will work in collaboration with First Nations and Inuit on this issue,” said Lauréanne Fontaine, press secretary to Quebec’s Minister of Indigenous Affairs, Sylvie D’Amours. For Ghislain Picard, Chief of the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador, the <l1>statements by Ms. D’Amours and Mr. Legault</l1> indicate that Quebec will leave little room for good-faith negotiation.
« M. Legault a déjà déclaré qu’il n’étai: “Mr. Legault has already said there is no question of First Nations having a veto. He imagines that the Wet’suwet’en situation is specific to British Columbia and that there can’t be similar situations here in Quebec. Obviously, in our view, Mr. Legault is way off base. All it would take is for a community with rights over a territory to block a major project for Quebec to realize that the rights of the Wet’suwet’en are no different from those of many nations in Quebec.”
<strong>Années 1970</strong> : La DNUDPA: 1970s: UNDRIP has its origins in the late 1970s, in resistance to the Canadian government and its police repression, and to its non-recognition of Indigenous rights, in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1976).
‍<strong>2007 </strong>: Pas moins de 14: ‍2007 : No fewer than 144 countries adopt UNDRIP, but Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand oppose it. To clear its name, then–Prime Minister Stephen Harper offers an apology to residential school survivors.
Cet épisode marque le début du processus: This episode marks the beginning of the process of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada.
‍<strong>2010</strong> : Le gouvernement: ‍2010: The government changes course and decides to adopt UNDRIP.
‍<strong>2015 : </strong>Le nouveau gouv: ‍2015: The new Liberal government calls for the implementation of UNDRIP. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission tables its report, which includes 94 recommendations – notably on the implementation of UNDRIP – and finds that Canada’s residential schools were responsible for a cultural genocide.
‍<strong>2016 :</strong> La ministre des: ‍2016: Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations Carolyn Bennett announces at the plenary session of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues that Canada fully supports the Declaration.
Russ Diabo et la plupart des Autochtones: Russ Diabo and most of the Indigenous Canadians in the room, however, feel she contradicts herself by adding that Canada will implement the Declaration in accordance with the Canadian Constitution.
